nameStory: The Kaston Sac Spider gets its name from renowned arachnologist Dr. Burtch Julian Kaston, who made significant contributions to North American spider identification in the mid-1900s. Like other sac spiders, it builds silken retreats or 'sacs' rather than traditional webs, creating cozy hideaways under bark or in leaf litter. Having a spider named after you is quite an honor in the arachnology world!
description: The Kaston Sac Spider is a small, nimble hunter that belongs to the leafcurling sac spider group. These spiders are typically pale yellowish to light brown in color with a somewhat elongated body shape. They're small spiders, usually measuring less than half an inch in total length including their legs. Rather than spinning webs to catch prey, they actively hunt at night and retreat to silken sacs during the day.

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Creates tubular silken retreats or sacs rather than catching webs - look for small, white, papery tubes tucked under loose bark or in leaf crevices that feel smooth and slightly stretchy to the touch

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Elongated, somewhat flattened body with relatively long legs that give it a sleek, streamlined appearance - feels smooth if gently touched

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Pale yellowish to light brown coloration with subtle darker markings on the abdomen - colors often appear almost translucent in good light

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small spider with body length typically under 6mm, with total leg span rarely exceeding 12mm - about the size of a small button

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Active nighttime hunter that moves quickly when disturbed - during day retreats to its silken sac and can be sluggish when first exposed

habitat: Look for Kaston Sac Spiders in wooded areas where they hide under loose tree bark, particularly on deciduous trees like oak and maple. They also inhabit leaf litter in forest floors and can sometimes be found under stones or fallen logs. These spiders prefer somewhat moist environments but not waterlogged areas, making mixed hardwood forests their ideal New England habitat.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, emerging from winter retreats and beginning to hunt more actively. Look for fresh silken sacs appearing under bark.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period with adults hunting nocturnally and creating new sacs regularly. This is the best time to find them by gently peeling back loose bark during the day.
seasonality.fall: Mating season occurs with egg sacs being produced. Adults may be more visible as they search for mates and suitable overwintering sites.
seasonality.winter: Adults retreat to protected locations like deep bark crevices or leaf litter, becoming dormant. They're rarely seen unless you dig through insulated hiding spots.

funFact: Despite being called 'leafcurling' sac spiders, most Clubiona species don't actually curl leaves - they got this name because early naturalists often found them in naturally curled dead leaves that made perfect ready-made hideouts!
confusionNotes: The Kaston Sac Spider can be easily confused with other Clubiona species in New England, especially the more common Canada Sac Spider. The key difference is often habitat preference and subtle size differences, but definitive identification usually requires microscopic examination of reproductive structures by an expert.
contextualKnowledge: With only one recorded observation in New England, the Kaston Sac Spider is either extremely rare in our region or significantly under-reported due to identification challenges. Many sac spiders in the Clubiona genus are difficult to distinguish without expert examination, so what appears to be other species might sometimes be misidentified Kaston Sac Spiders.
compareHints: Among its Clubiona relatives in New England, the Kaston Sac Spider is most similar to the Canada Sac Spider but tends to be slightly smaller and paler. Unlike the Riparian Sac Spider which prefers areas near water, the Kaston Sac Spider sticks to drier woodland habitats. The subtle differences between Clubiona species often require expert identification using microscopic features.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Clubiona spiralis is most similar to other Clubiona species like the Canada Sac Spider and Riparian Sac Spider, sharing the same general pale coloration and body proportions.
Unlike the Canada Sac Spider which prefers drier woodland habitats, the riparian sac spider sticks close to water sources.

Clubiona obesa stands out from its relatives like the Canada Sac Spider and Riparian Sac Spider by its notably thick, swollen abdomen - while other Clubiona species have more typical slender abdomens.
Compared to its inland relatives like the Canada sac spider or riparian sac spider, the maritime sac spider is distinguished primarily by its coastal habitat preference.
Bishop's Sac Spider differs from its more common relatives like the Canada Sac Spider and Riparian Sac Spider primarily in its rarity and subtle coloration differences.
Compared to other Clubiona species in New England, the Canada Sac Spider tends to favor slightly drier woodland habitats than the Riparian Sac Spider, which prefers areas near water sources.
